projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merits

The goal of this project was to explore new types of measurements in electron microscopy and spectroscopy using quantum physics. To this end, the project develops ways to prepare, measure, and use both the wave-like and particle-like nature of free electrons traveling through the vacuum inside electron microscopes. 

We created a device in which single electrons travel two separated paths through the electron microscope. To do this, we made two nanofabricated gratings to coherently “split” the electron wave into two or more paths, such that each individual path traveled a superposition of two routes through the system.  This device is called an electron Mach-Zehnder interferometer, and it enables new experiments and measurements inside conventional electron microscopes. For example, we used this tool to demonstrate that the electron retains its wavelike nature – the superposition state – even when the electron interacted with a target object of study and transferred energy to it.  In this setup, a fast electron in a superposition of two paths passed on both the left and right side of a metallic nanoparticle. Both electron paths excited a dipole transition in the nanoparticle – in this case, an optical excitation called a surface plasmon polariton. We showed that the quantum superposition of the electron did not get destroyed due to this inelastic interaction with an environment – the wavefunction did not collapse - and interference between the two paths could still be observed in electrons. This has potential applications for electron spectroscopic measurements of materials. 

This project also demonstrated quantum-enhanced measurement technique known as “interaction-free” measurement in which an interferometer is used to detect a opaque object without interacting with it. This experiment was based on a thought experiment proposed by Elitzur and Vaidman in which an interferometer could be to used for “quantum interrogation” to detect the presence of a hypothetical object such as a bomb without triggering it. The electron interferometer was tuned such that one of the possible outputs was near zero under normal conditions due to destructive interference of the electron wavefunction. Yet when an object is introduced to block one path of the electron interferometer, electrons could now be detected in this dark output, providing information about the presence of the object without interacting with it. This measurement scheme can potentially be used to improve the image contrast sensitive samples in an electron microscope before the electron beam destroys it, providing a significant improvement when imagine the molecular structure of biological matter and pharmaceuticals. 

These results were published in peer-reviewed scientific articles in professional journals (including two Physical Review Letters), many referreed conference papers, and numerous presentations at international scientific conferences. Results were also communicated in published PhD dissertations and various invited seminars and colloquium talks.

Broader Impacts

The McMorran lab shared this research with non-scientists, novice physics students, and trained advanced PhD students in several ways. With NSF support, a summer bridge course was designed and implemented to engage first- and second-year undergraduate students on research. The grant supported lab and instrument costs associated with this course, which involved 11 undergraduates in summer 2021 and 5 undergraduates in 2022. In 2023, 3 undergraduates continued beyond summer working on related projects. This curriculum included new classroom activities and exercises for existing physics courses, such as the UO’s introductory calculus-based physics sequence, as well as dedicated summer projects courses. Four undergraduate students remained in the group and continued to work on research related to this project, two as part of the NSF REU program. Several undergraduates associated with the work were encouraged to attend the Microscopy and Microanalysis conference in Portland, Oregon. To share this with non-scientists, the McMorran lab communicated results in interviews for popular news articles and participated in several science outreach activities to engage the public in science discoveries. The major effort was leading science-themed booths at the Oregon Country Fair. Theses physics booths attract hundreds of visitors of all ages from a large range of backgrounds, politics, ancestry, beliefs, and socioeconomic status. Here the PI performed numerous physics demonstrations and answered wide-ranging questions about technology and physics. Seven physics PhD students contributed to the project and gained useful training, and are now beginning careers in high technology industry.

All project participants developed proficiency in theoretical and experimental physics, computational data analysis and simulation, technical writing, and scientific communication. Students participating in the project learned optical theory, hologram design, nanoscale engineering and fabrication, electron microscopy, and quantitative image and data analysis, and advanced software development. Graduate students prepared and delivered regular presentations at group meetings and gave oral presentations at international conferences. This general skill set and specific research knowledge developed while training students working on this project are both in high demand within industry, thus providing an immediate broader impact to society.

abstractText:
The fastest-changing regions of the Antarctic and Greenland Ice Sheets that contribute most to sea-level rise are underlain by soft sediments that facilitate glacier motion. Glacier ice can infiltrate several meters into these sediments, depending on the temperature and water pressure at the base of the glacier. To understand how ice infiltration into subglacial sediments affects glacier slip, the team will conduct laboratory experiments under relevant temperature and pressure conditions and compare the results to state-of-the-art mathematical models. Through an undergraduate research exchange between University of Wisconsin-Madison, Dartmouth College, and the College of Menominee Nation, Native American students will work on laboratory experiments in one summer and mathematical theory in the following summer.

Ice-sediment interactions are a central component of ice-sheet and landform-development models. Limited process understanding poses a key uncertainty for ice-sheet models that are used to forecast sea-level rise. This uncertainty underscores the importance of developing experimentally validated, theoretically robust descriptions of processes at the ice-sediment interface. To achieve this, the team aims to build on long-established theoretical, experimental, and field investigations that have elucidated the central role of premelting and surface-energy effects in controlling the dynamics of frost heave in soils.  Project members will theoretically describe and experimentally test the role of premelting at the basal ice-sediment interface. The experiments are designed to provide quantitative insight into the impact of ice infiltration into sediments on glacier sliding, erosion, and subglacial landform evolution.

projectOutComesReport:
Although it has long been recognized that sliding is responsible for most glacier motion,  we still lack predictive models for the controls on this dynamic process. Some of the fastest sliding, which is responsible for most ice discharge to the oceans, takes place over beds of  water-saturated sediments. This collaborative project was designed to test new model treatments for conditions that cause glacial ice to gradually sink downwards into the  pores between sediment grains, where it forms a layer of partially frozen fringe that affects sliding behavior in ways that  can be examined using controlled laboratory experiments. Our new experimentally validated treatments of sliding behavior should eventually lead to more accurate forecasts for how glacier motion is likely to contribute towards sea-level changes, and how rapidly to anticipate changes to mountain glaciers that play a vital role in water resources and ecological systems. Additional broader impacts of our work included introducing Native American  students, who are underrepresented in STEM fields, to cutting-edge glacier research, training an undergraduate  student in mathematical modeling, mentoring a graduate student in laboratory research, and aiding in the career development of two promising postdoctoral scholars. Major academic findings supported by this research award are summarized in 9 peer-reviewed journal articles that have been uploaded to the NSF-PAR Repository; several additional journal articles that build upon the findings of this work are anticipated over the coming years. Project successes include the experimental growth of frozen fringe beneath sliding ice, with successful comparison to model treatments and control experiments conducted in a different apparatus designed to prohibit ice motion. Our sliding experiments led to the discovery   of a previously unknown mobile mushy zone of loosely ice-bound sediments that was able to deform at slower speeds and significantly affect the bed resistance. In addition to the construction of a predictive model that captures the observed dependence of bed resistance on experimental conditions, further model developments included a new  formulation that allows us to describe how the fringe develops in a more numerically efficient manner than in previous work, and also an extended treatment that accounts for sediment particle rearrangements as the forces communicated between adjacent particles change. We communicated these and other findings in talks at several universities and  conferences, culminating at the close of the grant period on August 4, 2024 in a pair of invited talks by University of Wisconsin Madison PI Lucas Zoet and University of Oregon PI Alan Rempel at the Gordon Conference on Rock Deformation, which brought together an international group of researchers who study the related  processes that control the deformation in Earth's Mantle that facilitates Plate Tectonics, the motion on faults that results in earthquakes and other slip processes, and the slip near Earth's surface that produces landslides.

abstractText:
The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic not only threatens the health and safety of communities but also the operation and survival of firms and industries that provide essential products and services to the innovative ecosystem. This crisis has hit small businesses (firms with fewer than 500 employees) particularly hard. Obtaining access to emergency financial resources such as the Paycheck Protection Program and forgivable loans offered by federal and state government agencies remains extremely difficult for many U.S. small firms. This holds especially for firms owned by members of underrepresented groups that include minorities, women, and veterans. This project has two primary aims in tracking the different types of small high-tech firms. First, we aim to understand the unique challenges and opportunities that small high-tech firms face in adapting to this unexpected shift and in introducing innovations designed to combat COVID-19. Second, we aim to evaluate state and federal responses to the pandemic by estimating their impacts on the activity of small high-tech firms that drive U.S. innovation. We plan to construct a comprehensive and scalable nationwide database that tracks U.S. small high-tech firms that are current or potential suppliers of critical public heath technologies related to pandemic response. We will make this database publicly available to accelerate broad systematic research. Our results will include detailed insights on the impacts of the pandemic on small business performance. Moreover, the resulting public databases and interactive dashboard will enable policymakers and businesses to identify new opportunities to empower small high-tech firms to grow and supply much needed expertise and resources during the pandemic.   

We examine the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the U.S. innovative ecosystem. We focus on small high-tech firms (with fewer than 500 employees), including firms owned by members of underrepresented groups (minorities, women, and veterans). Small firms are potential sources of innovation in combating COVID-19, but remain especially vulnerable to the unprecedented health, social, and economic risks arising from this pandemic. We have two primary research aims. First, we seek to characterize changes in the landscape of small high-tech firms resulting from the ongoing pandemic and policy responses. We will build a comprehensive, interactive database to capture shifts in the spatial and temporal patterns of the innovation ecosystem. Second, we seek to use this database for econometric analysis to evaluate the differential impact of state and federal pandemic policies on the performance of small high-tech firms. Specific deliverables include: (i) detailed descriptive statistics characterizing changes in concentrations of business activity in different sectors with geographic precision; (ii) a public dashboard with an interactive map for visualizing changes in the innovative ecosystem at state- and sector-levels; (iii) a public data repository providing access to all aggregated data files used to create our visualization tool; and (iv) econometric models exploiting variation in state policies to determine the causal impacts of these policies on small firms. Our intended broader impact is a clearer picture of which areas of the innovative ecosystem are most susceptible to the effects of COVID-19. We will identify firm-level characteristics that indicate which firms are most and least resilient, as well as those best positioned to assist with government countermeasures against the pandemic. This will illuminate priorities for public and private sector efforts to rebuild innovative activity and allocate support resources more effectively.

projectOutComesReport:
High-tech ventures play a central role not only in producing scientific contributions, but also in translating innovations to yield economic value. Yet, tracing such activity in a rigorous and systematic manner is challenging. This is most notably due to data constraints in tracking the activity of young ventures.

With support from the National Science Foundation, we drew upon rich and heretofore relatively untapped data to identify a critical population of young firms – specifically, ventures that seek to transact with the U.S. federal government. As our core data, we pulled administrative federal records available via the System for Awards Management (SAM) and their procurement activity as reported in USASpending.gov. We augmented this granular data with an extensive set of economic and demographic indicators (collected at the firm, census tract, county, state, and national levels). With this data, we have been able not only to examine a unique and valuable angle of the U.S. innovative ecosystem, but also to unpack changes in the landscape and trace the contributions of high-tech ventures.

For this project, we achieved the following aims: (i) characterizing the national ecosystem of innovative U.S. high-tech ventures; (ii) evaluating the impacts of policy decisions on that ecosystem; and (iii) publishing a comprehensive, flexible database tracing the population of U.S. ventures that are part of the innovative ecosystem. The public platform includes a dashboard with customizable mapping functionalities designed as a reference for scientists and policymakers, as well as interested citizens (APPRISE Platform website: https://appriseplatform.org).

The results from this project are manifold. As a baseline, we examine the antecedent factors that motivate ventures to initiate engagement with the government. Paying attention to a range of external and internal factors to the firm, we find evidence that areas with greater access to capital infrastructure decrease the rate of firm-government engagement, while firm-based growth capabilities increase such choice. Figure 1 illustrates the geographic distribution of all U.S. high-tech ventures in contrast to the sub-set of ventures that initiated firm-government engagement.  

Building upon this work, we examine the interactions of such ventures with the U.S. federal government. Prior work chiefly emphasizes firm-government transactions involving the government providing resources as a key input for firms via grants, subsidies, and loans. Yet, the scale and nature of interactions of ventures with their governments suggest that such characterization of firm-government relationships is missing or overlooking a different, but critical form of engagement. Governments can also serve as customers for ventures (i.e., purchasing key output from firms). Our empirical analyses of over 200,000 ventures reveal intriguing performance trends. We observe a significant financial upside for these firms. Moreover, these firms tend to provide services and support to the federal government rather than seek services and support from the federal government.

Furthermore, in tracing broader trends of the innovative ecosystem, we turn to U.S. cities. While the number and activity of high-tech ventures are important metrics in determining the overall health of surrounding innovative and economic conditions, ecosystems benefit from having higher levels of equity in the distribution of entrepreneurial resources. Yet current conditions are far from equitable. We document resource disparities, most notably among financial lending institutions in supporting minority-owned high-tech ventures.

abstractText:
Difficulty hearing and producing new sounds in a second language leads to lowered comprehension of the target language and difficulty speaking in a way that can be easily understood by native speakers. This can lead to painful interactions and potential abandonment of the acquisition effort. Research and anecdotal evidence highlight the difficulty that speakers of non-tonal languages have when attempting to form novel tone categories in other languages. Results from the proposed research will provide a greater understanding of the factors that affect the process of acquisition of novel tone categories, benefitting both learners and teachers. Factors tested in the proposed experiments are specific to pedagogical considerations when introducing novel suprasegmental categories. With greater foundational knowledge regarding these issues, language teachers will have a wider range of tools with which they will be able to develop optimal methodologies for helping their students better acquire tone categories.

Second language acquisition differs from first language acquisition in that it is possible to exogenously direct the learner’s attention to the target sound categories. However, even in second language acquisition, the majority of exposure to novel sound categories in the natural world occurs incidentally through interactions with native speakers and media, rather than through explicit instruction in a lab or in the classroom. Therefore, it is important to understand factors that affect the incidental formation of novel sound categories in natural speech. The proposed studies investigate factors affecting the incidental acquisition of novel tone categories by having learners focus on a simple visual matching task with tokens from the target auditory categories providing predictive clues about the location of the visual targets. This incidental learning paradigm permits the examination of factors known to affect novel sound category learning during explicit, directed training. A greater knowledge of factors impacting novel tone category formation during incidental learning will provide a contrastive evaluation of our knowledge of novel sound category formation during training with explicit instructions, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of how humans process speech sounds and form new sound categories.

projectOutComesReport:
Difficulty forming novel sound categories in a second language leads to lowered comprehension of the target language and difficulty producing novel sounds in a way that can be easily understood by native speakers. This can lead to painful interactions and potential abandonment of the effort to learn the language. Research and anecdotal evidence highlight the difficulty that speakers of non-tonal languages have when attempting to learn tone categories in a new language. Substantial research has addressed factors impacting the ability to learn novel sound categories during exposure to a second language. However, most studies examine learning under explicit, directed training. Explicit learning methods can be costly in time and resources as participants have to return for training over several weeks, potentially limiting the amount of research that can be done. By contrast, relatively few studies have examined the formation of novel sound categories under incidental conditions, where a person learns novel sound categories indirectly, while focused on another task. Previous research on incidental learning of synthesized sound categories indicates that humans can learn novel sound categories quickly and accurately via incidental learning. In this project we used an incidental learning paradigm to train monolingual English speakers on four Thai tone categories using naturally produced words. Specifically, participants heard sounds from one of four tone categories before the appearance of a visual target in one of four locations on the screen. The task was to click on the target quickly. As they learned to predict the location of the target using the sounds as cues, they became faster, and at the same time, they were learning to differentiate the tones into categories. They were then tested by hearing the sounds and guessing where the visual target should appear. After thirty minutes of training participants were able to accurately differentiate the four tone categories with up to 100 percent accuracy. The results of the study suggest that participants can form novel tone categories during incidental learning with natural words quickly and accurately. These results have significance for research and for language acquisition more broadly. The rapid learning of sound categories can increase the amount of research that can be done regarding factors that impact learning. In this study we also investigated multiple factors impacting learning. We found that variability within trial impacts incidental learning, with high variability of tokens within trial resulting in significantly higher accuracy scores. We found that initial exposure to a single talker during training results in significantly higher accuracy scores than hearing multiple talkers. We found that segmental familiarity in the tone bearing unit did not impact accuracy scores. We also found that production during perceptual learning significantly lowered accuracy scores. These results provide a greater understanding of the factors that affect the process learners go through as they form novel tone categories, benefitting both learners and teachers. Factors tested in the proposed experiments are specific to pedagogical considerations when introducing novel tone categories. With greater foundational knowledge regarding these issues, language teachers will have a wider range of tools with which they will be able to develop optimal methodologies for helping their students better acquire tone categories.

abstractText:
The evolution of novel traits can change the way that organisms interact with their environments to survive, grow and reproduce. Deep knowledge of the underlying genes and developmental changes that underly most evolutionary innovations is sparse, as is understanding of the ecological consequences for both the organisms in which novel traits emerged and the organisms with which they interact in communities. A particular gap in understanding is how the evolution of novel traits influences the biodiversity of their associated microbial communities. This project will help fill this gap in our knowledge by studying a remarkable innovation – male pregnancy in seahorses, pipefish and seadragons. This project will include the creation of new genome sequences and detailed studies of the developmental genetic underpinnings of the embryo brooding structures that make male pregnancy possible. The consequences of pouch evolution on the complexity and function of the community microbes in the pouch will also be studied, as well as how this unique host-associated microbiota can affect the fitness of embryos in the pouch. This project will provide research training to high school students, teachers, and undergraduates from underrepresented groups through immersive outreach and targeted support programs. The project will also support training of the next generation of scientists via education of Ph.D. students and postdoctoral scholars. Outreach to general public will be accomplished through public talks and through creation of a museum exhibit on syngnathid biology paired with web resources to support K-12 education.

Male pregnancy, accompanied by morphologically diverse embryo brooding structures, is a defining evolutionary innovation in syngnathid fishes. The goal of this project is to build an integrative understanding of the developmental genetic origin of this remarkable syngnathid novelty and its role in mediating multi-level ecological interactions with host-associated microbiota. This project will include production of 19 new annotated reference genomes strategically sampled across the syngnathid lineage, morphogenetic analysis and transcriptional/epigenetic profiling of the developing pouch in a comparative framework that leverages the repeated, independent evolution of complex brooding structures in the family, and analysis of brood pouch biocomplexity as a determinant of pouch-associated microbiome assembly. When complete, this project will provide novel insights into genome structural evolution in syngnathids, identify protein sequence and gene regulation changes involved in brood pouch development, and address whether the evolution of the brooding tissues created specialization in host regulation of microbiota with consequences for brooded progeny. The work will attract new researchers to syngnathids for studies of evolutionary innovation and diversification. The project will provide research training to high school students, teachers, and undergraduates from underrepresented groups, and will support education of graduate students and postdoctoral scholars, including the opportunity to take intense short courses to learn next generation sequencing, bioinformatics, complex statistical analyses, and genome editing. Educational outreach to general public will be accomplished through public lectures by the PIs, and through creation of a museum exhibit on syngnathid biology, which will be paired with an associated web resource directed toward K-12 education.

projectOutComesReport:
Novel traits of organisms are often associated with evolutionary diversification in lineages. However, the molecular and developmental mechanisms by which these evolutionary innovations are formed, and how they affect biodiversity at multiple levels, are poorly understood. We know little about the developmental genetic basis and functional consequences of all but a few evolutionary innovations. Many questions remain. For instance, do novelties necessarily arise from major "rewiring" of gene regulatory networks, and if so how? And do specific rules govern the ecological consequences for both the organisms that have evolved the novelties and the other organisms with which they interact in communities? Our project addressed these big questions.

A particular gap in our understanding of innovations of multicellular hosts is how the evolution of these traits influences the biodiversity of their associated microbial communities. Nearly all organisms on the planet have associated communities of microbes that can have significant effects on the fitness of the host. Every animal hosts trillions of bacteria, collectively called the microbiome, which help with digestion, immunity, and other vital functions. To fill this knowledge gap we performed an integrative study of the teleost fish family Syngnathidae, which comprises over 300 amazing species of seahorses, pipefish, and seadragons. These animals are among the most unusual and captivating fish in the ocean. Unlike nearly all other animals, it is the males who become pregnant and give birth to live young. This remarkable role reversal has fascinated scientists and the public alike for centuries. In addition, syngnathid males have evolved diverse traits in which to brood the offspring. Different species of syngnathids have developed the brooding traits to varying degrees; from simple skin flaps where eggs attach, to fully enclosed pouches that function much like a mammalian uterus, complete with nutrient transfer and immune protection for developing embryos. Our research project set out to understand how this extraordinary form of reproduction develops and learn more about the microbiomes in the pouch of diverse lineages. 

Our most significant scientific achievement for this project was the collection, sequencing, annotation and analysis of the complete genomes of 26 different syngnathid species, as well as 2 outgroup species. By comparing these 28 high-quality genetic blueprints across species, we identified genes that changed in syngnathids in surprising ways. We discovered that syngnathids have lost or modified many genes related to the immune system; changes that may help male fish tolerate embryos without rejecting them as foreign tissue. We discovered novel genes involved in bone development. We also pioneered new techniques for studying which genes are active in tissues such as head and jaws and the brood pouch during pregnancy. Using cutting-edge single cell sequencing technology, we examined gene activity in tens of thousands of individual cells of tissues. We discovered that important gene losses have led to rewiring of gene regulatory networks in key cell types. Another important discovery involved the microscopic communities of bacteria that live in and on these fish. We found that the brood pouch has its own distinct microbial community, different from the rest of the body, that changes during pregnancy and likely playing an important role in embryo health.

Beyond advancing scientific knowledge, this project achieved several additional goals. We trained several members of the next generation of researchers. We mentored undergraduate students, graduate students, postdoctoral scholars, and research scientists. Several trainees have gone on to faculty positions, careers in biotechnology and graduate school. We also worked to share our findings with the public. Our research on the spectacular leafy and weedy seadragons was covered by the New York Times and other major news outlets. At the University of Oregon, we ran hands-on science activities for middle school girls, introducing them to these fascinating fish and the scientists who study them. The broad genomic resources we created of over two dozen genome assemblies are now all freely available to researchers worldwide via the repository NCBI. These will help support conservation efforts for these vulnerable fish. Many syngnathid species are threatened by habitat loss, pollution, and overharvesting for traditional medicine and the aquarium trade. Understanding their genetics helps identify distinct populations that need protection and provides tools for monitoring wild populations. 

In summary, this project demonstrated that studying unusual animals can reveal fundamental principles about how complex traits evolve. Male pregnancy in syngnathids shares surprising similarities with pregnancy in mammals, showing that evolution often finds comparable solutions to shared challenges. By decoding the genomes of these remarkable fish, we gained new insights into reproduction, immunity, and the microbiome that extend far beyond syngnathids to inform our understanding of biology more broadly.

abstractText:
Ecological communities consist of species that interact with each other in many ways. An interaction in which both species benefit is called a "mutualistic" interaction.  For example, in pollination plants receive pollen to produce seeds and the pollinators receive food.  Some pollination partnerships may be unique and specialized, with each species depending on services that can be provided only by a single partner. Other pollination partnerships may be general and interchangeable, with many species providing the same services. If all partnerships are interchangeable, then communities may remain stable if their species change due to environmental stress. But if partnerships are unique and specialized, then communities may be very sensitive to stress. Thus, understanding how species interact in the way they do is a central question in ecology. This research will explore how different types of interactions (unique and specialized vs. interchangeable and generalized) affect how well plants and pollinators reproduce and how long their populations can persist in the face of environmental change. The study will focus on the plants and pollinators of the Madrean "sky islands", mountaintop meadows separated by lowland deserts in the southwestern United States. The study will help guide conservation and management of these unusual habitats and provide mentoring of students interested in ecological field work.

Network theory predicts that highly redundant and generalized networks of interactions maximize resistant to disturbance, whereas specialized, complementary networks maximize function. While such tradeoffs are assumed to be an inherent part of biological network organization, it is not known what ecological and evolutionary processes mediate them, preserving populations and maintaining network structure. Further, though interactions may be heterogeneous across both organismal (individual to species) and temporal scales (single interactions to multiple interactions across generations), the potential for this variability to drive both network structure and ecological function has not been systematically explored. This research will forge new ground by testing how mechanisms at different levels of biological organization simultaneously confer function and resistance within networks. By quantifying individual- and species-level networks, along with short- and long-term fitness outcomes, the researchers will examine the relationship between network structure, function and resistance, and their impact on plant and animal population dynamics across a biogeographic gradient.

abstractText:
NONTECHNICAL SUMMARY

Metal-organic frameworks are a family of highly crystalline and porous materials, constructed from molecular building blocks. Most metal-organic frameworks have been assumed to be defect-free scaffolds that glean their properties from their highly ordered, repeating chemical structures. However, it is becoming increasingly clear that defects may play a more important role in determining the properties of these materials than so far assumed. This award supports research utilizing computational materials and chemistry techniques to examine the opportunities that emerge from defect sites in metal-organic frameworks.  The PI will employ state-of-the-art computational methods to examine defects that give rise to increased electronic conductivity in the scaffolds, which could enable novel energy storage technologies, as well as defects that create sites to append and perform catalytic transformations. 

This award also supports strengthening the PI's existing outreach program centered around improving scientific literacy by teaching chemistry through the lens of coffee. In particular, the PI will (i) create an open-source library of peer-reviewed coffee-related scientific articles and write single-page summaries of the articles' key data and learning outcomes, and (ii) organize a seminar tour in African coffee-producing countries with the purpose of increasing awareness of the PI's work, recruiting students, and learning from these communities.

TECHNICAL SUMMARY

Metal-organic frameworks are an emergent class of porous, solid-state materials whose properties are widely thought to be determined by their bulk composition and topologies. Previous work has shown that electronic structure calculations on the crystallographic structures are instructive in predicting both photophysical properties and electronic properties in a wide variety of scaffolds. However, it is becoming increasingly clear that defects may play a more major role in determining the properties of these materials than so far assumed. This award supports computational research aimed at assessing the thermodynamic, electronic, and photophysical properties of a range of known defective scaffolds through the application of first principles defect calculations. The research activities include i) an exploration of the impact of vacancies and interstitials, and the emergent electronic properties associated with these defects; ii) examine hydrogenic interstitial-coupled electron transfer reactions that will enable both n- and p-type doping in the series of known conductive metal-organic frameworks; and iii) examination of hydrogenic/cationic defects in insulating metal-organic frameworks as a route to stabilizing exotic oxidation states through population of the conduction band. 

This award also supports strengthening the PI's existing outreach program centered around improving scientific literacy by teaching chemistry through the lens of coffee. In particular, the PI will (i) create an open-source library of peer-reviewed coffee-related scientific articles and write single-page summaries of the articles' key data and learning outcomes, and (ii) organize a seminar tour in African coffee-producing countries with the purpose of increasing awareness of the PI's work, recruiting students, and learning from these communities.

Diamonds consist of a regular arrangement, or lattice, of carbon atoms, which often contains defects at the atomic level.  Common defects include impurities, such as nitrogen or silicon atoms, and vacancies - places in the lattice where atoms are missing.   A special defect is a “silicon-vacancy” center, which consists of two vacancies that are adjacent to each other, with a silicon atom inserted in between.  An electron can be trapped around such a defect, and used as a “qubit,” or “quantum bit”—a fundamental unit of quantum information.  An outstanding challenge for using these qubits to develop solid-state quantum computers is the precise control of the interactions between them.  This program will develop an experimental approach that uses mechanical vibrations in an ultrathin diamond film to mediate interactions between two silicon-vacancy qubits.  Mechanical waves can be conveniently confined and guided in a suitably designed solid-state nanostructure with negligible loss, opening up a new frontier in the development of quantum information technologies.  In addition, this program will also make contributions to education and human resources by providing excellent training to graduate and undergraduate students in areas of both scientific and technological importance.

This experimental program focuses on mechanically mediated coupling between electron spins in a diamond nanomechanical resonator, with the long-term goal of establishing a trapped-ion-like solid-state platform for quantum computing.  The primary building block of this platform is a diamond Lamb wave mechanical resonator, in which electron spins in silicon vacancy centers couple to a symmetric mechanical compression mode.  The Lamb wave resonator is protected by a phononic crystal lattice, which can enable the achievement of mechanical Q-factors limited only by the intrinsic material loss of diamond.  Two mechanisms that take advantage of the special energy level structure of silicon vacancy centers will be explored for the coupling between spins and mechanical vibrations.  One exploits optically driven sideband spin transitions.  The other uses mechanical vibrations to directly drive spin transitions.  The sideband spin transitions will be used for spin entanglement through a Molmer-Sorensen two-qubit gate, which is widely used for trapped ions.  The direct acoustic driving will be used for spin entanglement via a phononic cavity QED process.

projectOutComesReport:
Diamond consists of a regular array or a lattice of carbon atoms as well as an extremely small number of defects in the carbon lattice, including impurities, such as nitrogen or silicon atoms, and vacancies - places in the lattice where atoms are missing.  Suitable combinations of impurities and vacancies can lead to the formation of color centers, which interact with light and give color to an otherwise transparent diamond.  A special color center is a “silicon-vacancy (SiV)”, which consists of two adjacent vacancies with a silicon atom inserted in between.  An electron trapped in such a color center can serve as a quantum bit or simply a qubit, which is a fundamental unit of quantum information.  An outstanding challenge for using these qubits to develop quantum computers is to precisely control the interactions between the qubits.

This research program at the University of Oregon has explored the use of mechanical vibrations to mediate interactions between two SiV qubits, with the long-term goal of developing an experimental platform for solid-state quantum computers.  A key building block of this platform is a thin (about 500 nanometers in thickness) rectangular diamond plate (a few micrometers in lateral dimensions), which serves naturally as a mechanical resonator and features compressional mechanical vibrations or modes with a frequency ranging from one to several GHz. The mechanical modes of the thin elastic plate are characterized by the so-called Lamb waves or Lamb modes.  The thin elastic plate is thus referred to as a Lamb wave resonator (LWR). 

The LWRs can be embedded in or attached to an artificially engineered square lattice with a spatial period of several micrometers.  A frequency gap in the mechanical vibration modes in this square lattice can isolate and protect the mechanical modes in the LWR from its surrounding environment, eliminating mechanical losses other than the intrinsic material loss of diamond.  LWRs with a fundamental compression mode frequency as high as 4 GHz have been successfully fabricated from a single-crystal diamond film with an initial thickness about 30 micrometers (see Figure 1).   

An all-optical approach to excite and detect the fundamental compression mode in a diamond LWR has been developed.  The compression mode is excited with the temporally modulated optical gradient force of a sharply focused laser beam (see Figure 2).  The induced vibrations are detected via their interactions with a SiV center.  Experimental studies carried out at temperatures of a few Kelvins show that the linewidth of the mechanical resonance for 1-GHz LWRs can be below 100 Hz, corresponding to a mechanical quality factor exceeding 10 million.  These results indicate that the diamond LWRs can be used for controlling the interactions between a SiV qubit and a mechanical mode at the level of single quanta of the mechanical vibrations, which is a crucial requirement for using mechanical vibrations to mediate and control the coupling between qubits. The ultrahigh mechanical quality factor achieved also shows that the artificial square lattice employed can provide a nearly ideal protection for the mechanical mode. 

An architecture for a mechanical network of LWRs has also been developed, for which three different schemes or geometric configurations are used for the coupling between two adjacent LWRs.  The coupling can take place near the nodes of the two LWRs, between the antinodes of the two LWRs, or between the antinode of one LWR and the node of the other LWR.  The three coupling schemes effectively enable a large range of nearest neighbor coupling rates (from a few hundred MHz down to tens of kHz).  Combinations of these schemes can also enable the development of two-dimensional mechanical networks.  Furthermore, the frequency of each LWR in the network can be tailored by varying either the length or the width of the LWR. 

This mechanical network is characterized by the nearest neighbor coupling rate, J, as well as the onsite potential (i.e., the frequency of the individual resonators).  A mechanical Wannier-Stark (WS) ladder can be formed with a constant frequency offset, F, between adjacent mechanical resonators. The WS ladder features equally spaced resonance frequencies and localized wave functions for the collective mechanical vibrations.  The ratio, F/J, determines the degree of localization, and thus the corresponding connectivity of the mechanical network.  This type of mechanical network can enable extended-range network connectivity, providing a promising platform for exploring new generations of quantum error correction (QEC) codes, which can overcome the high overhead of QEC codes that only have the nearest neighbor connectivity.   

This research program has also made important contributions to education and human resources by providing training for graduate and undergraduate students in areas of quantum science and technology. Two graduate students supported by this program have graduated with PhD in physics.

abstractText:
An award is made to the University of Oregon Eugene to support the purchase of a high-throughput fluorescent slide-scanner imaging system.  High throughput analysis of biological specimens is increasingly essential for advancing many fields of the life sciences. A key bottleneck, particularly in the study of histological specimens, is the need for manual steps that limit the speed of data acquisition. The new slide scanning microscope will automate many of the manual steps to remove critical bottlenecks and enable high throughput analysis of biological specimens by researchers at the University of Oregon and beyond. The new instrument will be housed in the University of Oregon shared Histology and Genetic Modification Research Core Facility. As part of a core facility, this instrument will enhance training of undergraduate and graduate students and postdoctoral scholars with cutting edge microscopy approaches, advanced image analysis, “big data”, and other key quantitative skills.  The system will further accelerate student research during summer REU programs and will also be used in outreach programs and shared with neighboring institutions.

The new system will be used for a wide range of biological studies, including gene expression, anatomical reconstructions, and tissue analysis, as well as contributing to undergraduate and graduate coursework and training. Two features of this automated instrument will transform the ability of UO researchers to perform these types of studies.  First, it automatically images large area specimens, stitching together individual high magnification fields of view into a single high-resolution image. Second, it can automatically process a large number of specimens, with an autoloader capable of processing up to 200 slides in succession. These capabilities will allow researchers to acquire complete datasets that are simply not tractable with manual imaging, thereby opening up new types of biological questions. The instrument has both brightfield and fluorescent capabilities, enabling a wide range of applications including in situ hybridization analysis of gene expression, reconstruction of large-scale neural organization, and quantification of anatomical and cellular structures. Results from these studies will be disseminated in peer-reviewed journals, through presentation at scientific meetings, and as part of public outreach efforts.

projectOutComesReport:
High throughput analysis of large samples of biological specimens is becoming essential for advancing many fields of the life sciences. Many current biological questions no longer focus on just one cell or one gene, and therefore require characterization of complete tissues, or screening of large numbers of samples.  A key bottleneck, particularly in the study of histological specimens, is the lack of automated equipment that can dramatically speed of data acquisition, making such studies feasible. This proposal requested funds for the purchase of a slide scanning microscope, to perform high throughput analysis of biological specimens, for use by researchers at the University of Oregon and beyond. The purchased instrument is a Leica Aperio Versa, which is a complete system capable of automated acquisition of brightfield and fluorescence images, with slide-scanning capability allowing high throughput imaging of multiple fields of view in large numbers of specimens automatically. Two features of this automated instrument are transforming the ability of UO researchers to perform these types of studies. First, it automatically images large area specimens, stitching together individual high magnification fields of view into a single high-resolution image. Second, it can automatically process a large number of specimens, with an autoloader capable of processing up to 200 slides in succession. These capabilities allow researchers to acquire complete datasets that are simply not tractable with manual imaging, thereby opening up new types of biological questions.

The proposed instrument was purchased in August 2020, and installed in the Histology core facility, by Leica representatives in October 2020. During the installation, three staff members were directly trained in the use of the instrument and we coordinated with UO Information Technology to set up the network server in a central data center with appropriate connectivity. Together, this established full functionality of the microscope along with expertise to provide service to users. This therefore completed the major initial goal of this proposal. Our subsequent goal was to extend use of this instrument to users across campus. Because the installation/training process made it clear significant expertise would be needed to operate the microscope, we decided to have core facility staff perform imaging as a service, rather than individual users accessing the scope directly. We therefore established a system for users to provide samples, request specific imaging configurations, and receive data back. We also established a re-charge system to cover the expenses associated with microscope usage and staff time. We did encounter multiple malfunctions of the instrument that resulted in it being inoperable for significant periods of time, but these have been resolved for now.

To date, we have had fifteen users, across four departments (Biology, Human Physiology, Psychology, Bioengineering), studying 6 different species (human, non-human primate, rabbit, mouse, zebrafish, octopus) with multiple techniques. The users also include a wide range of training level, from graduate students to faculty. We hope that this usage will continue to expand now that service issues with the instrument have been addressed.

The use of the instrument has resulted in one publication so far, a single-cell atlas of the octopus visual system, with other manuscripts in progress. Data from the microscope has been included in presentations to summer REU students and used for data analysis in an undergraduate programming course. Overall, the acquisition of this microscope has greatly expanded the capacity for high-throughput imaging at University of Oregon, which is having a significant impact on biological research and is being integrated into undergraduate education.

abstractText:
Kilauea (Hawai'i) is one of the world’s most active volcanoes. The volcano erupted continuously for 35 years between 1983 and 2018 covering a vast area and burying several communities. The activity that started in May 2018 marked the first time that lava erupted this far east of the summit of Kilauea since 1960, and it led to great anguish for the local population, authorities, and government monitoring agencies. The communities of Leilani Estates, Lanipuna Gardens, Kapoho, and Vacationland (a total of 715 homes) were successively covered by lava flows and tephra, before effusion mostly stopped in August 2018. This eruption stood out in terms of sheer volume, erupting the equivalent of 8 years of prior activity within just a 3-month timeframe. Chemical analyses of the May 2018 lava revealed the anomalous composition of the first lavas: they were not recently supplied to the volcano’s summit magma plumbing system, as normally occurs, but instead had been stored for decades or longer directly underneath those communities located on the eastern flanks of Kilauea. These stored magma pockets slowly cooled and evolved in composition through time, generating no recognizable seismic activity or volcanic gas releases. This collaborative project combines expertise from six different institutions and will investigate the chemical properties of lavas erupted at this site in 2018 and in older nearby eruptions (1790, 1840, 1955, 1960) to determine how long magma pockets can stay in eruptible form within these regions, and at what depths they likely reside. This information will be crucial in the years to come to better understand and inform the local population about hazardous phenomena for the Island of Hawai'i. A 3-day long workshop in Hilo (Hawai'i) involving 8 senior scientists, two graduate students, and a number of undergraduate students from two local universities will seek to communicate new information stemming from this project to academics and the public. Participation in K-12 activities in schools near the 2018 eruption site are proposed not only to offer background information on Kilauea hazards, but also for academics and researchers to gain deeper insight about the effects such eruptive crises have on local populations.

In detail, this project proposes to characterize droplets of melt that are trapped within crystals (olivine, pyroxene, plagioclase) during their growth in these older stored pockets of magma. These melt droplets (melt inclusions) preserve key chemical information about the stored magmas before they become modified by mixing with other magmas like in 2018. Chemical fingerprinting of the magma characteristics through different eruptions will help us understand whether these magmas are linked through time, and give first insights on their longevity within the lower east rift zone of Kilauea Volcano. Because melt inclusions also trap volatiles (H2O, CO2, S) whose concentrations depend directly on the depth of magma storage, quantifying these concentrations can be used to reconstruct storage pressure and depth of these magma pockets. Finally, three dimensional numerical models of cooling of magma bodies of different sizes and geometries under the rift zone will be combined with the geochemical information obtained to place tighter constraints on the timescales over which these magma pockets survive in eruptible form. At the time this project is starting, both Mauna Loa and Kilauea volcanoes show signs of magma input in their plumbing systems. Characterizing the complex subsurface magmatic structure of these shield volcanoes is therefore essential.

abstractText:
This CAREER award funds the research activities of Professor Tien-Tien Yu at the University of Oregon. 

After many years of increasingly compelling observational evidence, scientists have come to believe that most of the matter in the Universe is unlike the ordinary matter that we see and interact with every day.  This matter is called “dark matter” as it cannot be observed directly. Instead, the existence of dark matter is deduced through its gravitational effects on astrophysical objects such as stars and galaxies, which hints that it could be either a new type of particle or several different types of particles that together comprise a dark sector.  The fact that dark matter interacts gravitationally suggests that it has a mass, but the range of possible dark-matter masses is unknown. In recent years, research has facilitated an explosion of ideas and experimental efforts aimed at searching for dark-sector candidates across a wide range of masses.  In anticipation of the plethora of data and potential discoveries that will be enabled by these experimental efforts, Professor Yu will conduct an original research program focused on searching for and understanding a wide range of dark-sector theories in which she will elucidate the possible interpretations of a putative experimental signal.  Research on dark-sector physics advances the national interest by promoting the progress of science in one of its most fundamental directions:  the discovery and understanding of new physical law.

More technically, Professor Yu will unravel the dependence of dark-matter direct-detection rates on astrophysical uncertainties by applying a variety of different astrophysical models to dark matter-electron scattering calculations. In addition, she will develop a framework for presenting dark matter-electron scattering rates in a manner that is independent of the underlying astrophysical model, thereby circumventing the limitations on interpretation set by astrophysical uncertainties.  She will also uncover the potential of sub-GeV dark matter experiments by exploring the signatures of a broad range of theoretical models. Her work will allow for more robust interpretations of the experimental data and provide the foundational research for potential transformative discoveries. She will also explore in more detail the interplay between dark matter and gravitational waves, starting with a thorough calculation of neutron-star superradiance. This project is also envisioned to have significant broader impacts. Professor Yu will integrate her research and educational goals by developing a unique scientific communication program that aims to increase the accessibility of complex physics concepts through visual media. Comics and visual media provide a unique and accessible format to engage diverse audiences.  Professor Yu will develop a new program in visual scientific communication through collaboration with the University of Oregon’s strong Comic Studies program. By integrating visual media as the primary framework, this program aims to build skills and attitudes among underrepresented minority students in physics to enhance retention while simultaneously providing engaging, informal STEM education to a broad audience including humanities and design students.

projectOutComesReport:
This NSF award supported the research program of Principal Investigator Tien-Tien Yu, carried out in collaboration with postdoctoral fellows and graduate students. Understanding the nature of dark matter remains one of the most significant open questions in modern physics. While its existence is well established through astrophysical and cosmological observations, the particle nature of dark matter remains unknown. The research supported by this project sought to advance our understanding of dark matter by developing new theoretical frameworks and practical tools to probe its properties in previously unexplored ways.

Intellectual Merit - A central intellectual achievement of this project was the systematic expansion of the theoretical landscape of dark matter models and the development of connections between these models and experimentally testable signatures. These accomplishments fall into three main areas.

The first area focused on the direct detection of sub-GeV dark matter candidates. In this work, the PI and collaborators introduced new detection strategies that can leverage existing experimental platforms, along with innovative analysis methods such as halo-independent approaches and searches for daily modulation signals.

The second area investigated the cosmological signatures of ultralight scalar dark matter. This research examined how such candidates could influence early-universe processes, including Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and the formation of the Cosmic Microwave Background, thereby providing new avenues for constraining dark matter properties through cosmological observations.

The third area explored collider and accelerator probes of dark matter. This work examined experimental opportunities ranging from fixed-target experiments such as NA62 to future facilities including a proposed muon collider. The resulting studies provide detailed predictions for experimental signatures and offer concrete targets and strategies for experimentalists designing detectors and analysis techniques aimed at maximizing discovery potential.

Broader Impacts - A major broader-impacts outcome of this award was the establishment of the University of Oregon Comics and Science Fellowship. Each academic term, the fellowship supports two undergraduate students in comics studies who partner with a University of Oregon researcher to create an original work of comics art communicating the researcher’s work. To date, the program has produced more than fourteen science-focused comics that communicate research topics to broad audiences. These works are publicly available at: https://opentext.uoregon.edu/science-comics/

 In addition, the PI delivered several public lectures on dark matter over the course of the project, helping to communicate current developments in fundamental physics to general audiences and fostering broader public engagement with scientific research.

abstractText:
The development of clean and sustainable energy sources is critical for the economic and environmental vitality of human civilization. Renewables, such as sun and wind power, are intermittent and thus expensive to integrate with fossil fuels at the capacity needed to power the planet. Scalable, inexpensive energy-storage technologies are needed. In this project, Dr. Boettcher (University of Oregon) is collaborating with Dr. Ayers at Proton OnSite / Nel Hydrogen (Wallingford, Connecticut) to study the conversion of water (H2O) into hydrogen (H2) and oxygen (O2) gas using renewable electricity as the input. Hydrogen gas is a sustainable, carbon-free, renewable fuel to replace fossil fuels. It can be used in fuel cells to re-generate electricity on demand or burned like natural gas, without carbon dioxide emission. This research is addressing the inefficiency of the oxygen production part of the overall reaction. The team combines fundamental studies to understand how this reaction occurs and how to improve it. The industry-academic collaboration is testing the findings in commercially-relevant systems. In one example, the team is studying how chemical species containing iron, when placed in different environments, speed up the generation of oxygen and save energy in making hydrogen. The team is working to understand how these iron species change under long-term practical operating conditions. The team is also designing new materials that work well with existing technology but are less expensive to manufacture. The graduate students working on the project complete industry internships at Proton OnSite. The team conducts outreach activities with local middle school students that engages them in hands-on energy storage and sustainability laboratory activities on the University of Oregon campus, and introduces first year university students to scientific research through research-immersion courses. Funding for this award is provided by the Chemical Catalysis Program in the Division of Chemistry and the Catalysis Program in Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems.
 
Professor Shannon Boettcher from the University of Oregon (UO) is collaborating with Dr. Kathy Ayers at Proton OnSite / Nel Hydrogen (Wallingford, CT) and her team to use well-controlled electrochemical synthesis to create Fe in different local environments in transition-metal oxyhydroxide and oxide phases and probe OER mechanism and activity/durability relationships using a host of advanced operando techniques.  They uncover the compositional, structural, and morphological dynamics that drive performance degradation in (oxy)hydroxide/oxide OER catalysts under long-durations and high-current densities.  The team also creates new synthetic approaches to assemble precious-metal OER catalysts for use in proton-exchange-membrane electrolyzers where every precious metal atom is available to drive the OER while chemically stabilized by appropriate oxo linkages to inactive metal cations and through support interactions. This research has the potential to decouple the apparent inverse relationship observed between stability and activity for OER catalysts while connecting industry and academic researchers through graduate-student internships at Nel Hydrogen / Proton Onsite and industry researcher visits to Oregon. These science aims are coupled with outreach and education activities.  Graduate students lead teams of undergraduates through a “research-immersion” course developed by Boettcher that enables first-year chemistry students to earn credit for general chemistry laboratory by working on real, unsolved scientific questions.  Hands-on middle school outreach events in the area of energy and electrochemistry are available to underserved students through an ongoing program founded by Boettcher. Funding for this award is provided by the Chemical Catalysis Program in the Division of Chemistry and the Catalysis Program in Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems.

projectOutComesReport:
Water electrolysis is one of the major hydrogen production pathways being considered in the decarbonization economy given its potential for synergy with intermittent renewable electricity generation. Hydrogen produced through the electrochemical reduction of water offers a low-to-zero-emissions alternative to steam reforming of fossil fuels (methane) and a solution to curtailment. The principal source of inefficiency in the electrolysis process is related to the oxidative half-reaction (OER). This reaction can be made more efficient with the use of optimally designed catalysts based on earth-abundant elements, ultimately reducing the product cost. Over the past ten years the group of Boettcher has developed record-performance OER catalysts based on nickel, iron and cobalt and contributed to expanding the current understanding of the factors that govern their activity.

During the course of this project, the team continued to work on nickel and cobalt-based catalysts (oxyhydroxides). They discovered that introducing iron impurities to these materials under different oxidative conditions results in more or less active catalytic sites. When Fe is introduced to the catalyst under a strongly oxidizing potential, every Fe atom produces 10 times more oxygen than its typical value. The direct control on how active the Fe sites may be in these record catalysts provides a powerful tool for further investigations into the mechanism for oxygen evolution and the design of better catalysts for alkaline water electrolyzers. They also demonstrated how essentially any Ni-based catalysts, even when constrained in well-defined crystalline structures and in the presence of other elements will reconstruct at the outer interface to an amorphous Ni oxyhydroxide phase in highly oxidizing and alkaline environments. This finding points to an overarching relevance in understanding the catalytic mechanisms for OER on oxyhydroxides, which form independently of nominal crystal structure. Finally, they showed that while it is possible to design catalysts with a low total metal utilization (important when making use of precious-group-metals in acidic water electrolyzers), catalyst dissolution is still a major issue in acidic devices. We reported that even the addition of acid-stable protection layers can trigger dissolution events of both the catalyst and the substrate. Together, these results demonstrate that deeper level understanding of the catalytic mechanism reallycan point to design strategies for efficient, low-cost, improved catalyst materials and that accounting for dynamic changes of the catalyst-electrolyte system during operation is a necessary condition for any structure-function interpretation.

The team is also involved in recruiting, inspiring and educating the next generation of scientists through various activities. Graduate students supported by this grant developed and implemented an advanced laboratory project that directly touches upon key concepts from this and previous project cycles. The activity was geared toward incoming freshmen at the University of Oregon through Catalyst -- a no-cost summer bridge program intended to facilitate the high-school-to-college transition. The team has consistently conducted outreach activities with local underserved middle- and elementary-school students, engaging them in hands-on energy-storage and sustainability laboratory activities, promoting curiosity-driven exploration, granting exposure to real-life scientists and helping develop an "I can see myself as a scientist" self-image. Graduate students supported by this grant also developed and implemented research-immersion laboratory courses for first-year chemistry students at the University of Oregon. Participants in these courses earned general chemistry laboratory credit by working in teams of 3-4 on real research questions associated with this National Science Foundation grant.

abstractText:
The study of dynamical systems is the study of the long-term behavior of evolving systems. The modern theory of dynamical systems originated at the end of 19th century with fundamental questions concerning the stability and evolution of the solar system, which rapidly led to developments of applications to physics, biology, meteorology, economics and other areas. This project is a mathematical analysis of certain topological dynamical systems via C*-algebra theory. C*-algebras are infinite dimensional linear algebras. The project is an attempt to use a few computable data to determine the structure of certain C*-algebras arising from the dynamical systems. The project also studies closely related C*-algebra theory which will be used in the computation of data generated by dynamical systems. The success of the project would reveal the deep internal relationship between the theory of dynamical systems and theory of C*-algebras and pave the way for further applications of these theories.

The project may also be described as a study of theoretical applications of the classification of simple amenable C*-algebras to the study of topological dynamical systems. The central goal of the project is to use K-theory related data to analyze the structure of minimal dynamical systems and to develop new general methods to compute K-theory related groups for separable amenable C*-algebras. Let G be a group acting on a compact metric space X. The algebra of continuous functions on X together with the group action generate a crossed product C*-algebra. One specific problem that the project will study is to determine when two such actions are asymptotically conjugate. Closely related problems include the study of automorphisms on C*-algebras. It is proposed to use K-theory and KK-theory as well as tracial information to characterize the group actions. Methods developed in the theory of classification of simple amenable C*-algebras will be further enriched. Moreover new bridges between dynamical systems and C*-algebra theory will be built. The project will also study irreducible representations of certain simple C*-algebras. It is the proposer's long term goal to provide, from this project and related research as well as via related studies by other researchers, some deeper theoretical understandings and wider applications of C*-algebra theory and its interplay with the study of dynamical systems to various other related research areas, such as ergodic theory, non-commutative homotopy theory, abstract harmonic analysis, as well as physics and biology.

projectOutComesReport:
Project Outcomes Report


The main outcome of the project is the classification of separable simple amenable C*-algebras in the UCT class. Simple C*-algebras arise from   many fields of mathematics, notably in the classical dynamical systems,
operator theory, group representations and non-commutative geometry.
The main mathematical goal of the classification of simple C*-algebras is to use some limited and  computable data to completely determine the structure of these simple C*-algebras.  More technically speaking, we proved that two simple C*-algebras in the class are  the same (isomorphic) if and only if they have the same Elliott invariant.  This technical part is called the isomorphism theorem.
There were two main cases, the unital case and the stably projectionless case.
The unital part was published during the project supporting time.  The case of the classification of stably projectionless  is divided into  four  research papers, three of them have been published and one was posted.

As a part of the classification, we showed (by construction) that
every possible Elliott invariant can be achieved by some model C*-algebras. From the isomorphism theorem, when one applies C*-algebra theory,
one can use one's own choice  of the model C*-algebras that we constructed in place of any other C*-algebras in the class with the same Elliott invariant,
since any other C*-algebras in the class is isomorphic to one  of the model C*-algebras. During the time of  the  award,  the PI, together with PI's co-authors, solved a 15 years old open problem, namely, we showed that every Z-stable simple C*-algebra has stable rank one.

 Impacts
 
 In quantum mechanics, or in microscopical physical world, an observable may be modeled by a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space. A system of such operators forms a C*-algebra.  As mentioned above,
 C*-algebras arise from different branch of mathematics.  The success of the classification of separable simple C*-algebras provides the wide range of applications, in particular, in the topological dynamical systems in the immediate future. 

During the award time,  the PI had attended several conferences online introducing research results from the project and when the pandemic eased, the PI  and one of his students participated Great Plains Operator Theory Symposium  2022. The  PI also made several academic visits
 including  University of Erlangen, Germany, Canadian Operator Symposium  2022, The Fields  Institute for Mathematical Research, and Research Center for Operator Algebras.  A Ph.D. student in University of Oregon just defended the thesis on simple C*-algebras closely related to  the project. A graduate course in operator algebras is scheduled in University of Oregon in the fall of 2023 on topics related to this project. The results of the project also influence some of young researchers such as
 K. Li from Erlangen, X. Fu  in Toronto and J. Gabe currently in Odense and new reseacrh project has been developed to study non-simple C*-algebras.

abstractText:
The notion of linear dependence is fundamental to linear algebra, which in turn lies at the core of all branches of mathematics.   The theory of matroids is an abstraction of this notion.  While linear algebra provides many rich examples of matroids, one can prove that almost all examples of matroids are not realizable via linear algebra.  The main purpose of this project to show that two major theorems about realizable matroids in fact hold for all matroids. In addition the project will provide research training opportunities for graduate students.

The first of these theorems is the Top-Heavy Conjecture of Dowling and Wilson, which states that, given a matroid along with a natural number k that is at most half the rank, then the number of flats of rank k is less than or equal to the number of flats of corank k.  The second says that the coefficients of the Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomial of a matroid are all non-negative.  Both of these statements were proved for realizable matroids in the past five years by applying Hodge theory to the intersection cohomology groups of a certain algebraic variety associated with the realization.  The goal of this project is to show that, even though it is impossible to construct an analogous algebraic variety for a general matroid, one can still define analogues of its intersection cohomology groups and prove that they have enough nice properties to imply these two results.

projectOutComesReport:
A matroid is an object that encodes a combinatorial abstraction of the notion of linear dependence. The name derives from the word matrix: given a matrix, there is an associated matroid that records the rank of any subset of the columns. Not all matroids arise in this manner, but those that do form a large class of matroids that provide good intuition for matroids in general.


A subset of columns is called a flat if it adding any new column would increase the rank.  The Top Heavy Conjecture of Dowling and Wilson, formulated in 1976, says roughly that every matroid has more flats of high rank than of low rank.  The primary outcome of this project was a proof of this conjecture.

The proof involved constructing and studying a new object called the intersection cohomology of a matroid.  This is a powerful new tool, which has already had applications beyond the Top Heavy Conjecture.  In particular, we also used it to prove the non-negativity of the coefficients of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial of a matroid, which was conjectured in 2016 by Elias, Wakefield, and the PI.  Further applications are in the works.

The results of this project have been widely disseminated through preprints, publications, and lectures.  For example, the proof of the Top Heavy Conjecture was the subject of Okounkov's popular scientific exposition of the work of June Huh at the 2022 ICM; it is also the topic of a forthcoming expository article in the Notices of the AMS.
