projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit

Understanding the traits that distinguish humans from other species is one of the primary goals of biological anthropology. Arguably one of the most human traits is the way that we move. Humans are the only bipedal primate, and as a species we are among the best long-distance runners on Earth. This is due in part to the high proportion of slow myofibers within our skeletal muscles, which enhance muscle endurance and optimize them for endurance-based tasks like walking and running. This suggests that this trait was adaptive for long-distance bipedal locomotion, yet the genetic mechanisms underlying species-specific differences in muscle myofiber content were largely unknown. We hypothesized that human-specific mutations in regions of the genome that regulate the strength and timing of gene activity increase the expression of slow myofiber genes during development, leading to the slow-myofiber dominant muscles that distinguish our species. Given the relevance of slow myofibers to human locomotor performance, it is likely that these human-specific mutations were under selection in the hominin lineage. To address this gap in knowledge, we characterized regions of the genome active in mouse muscle and compared these regions across slow and fast-myofiber dominant muscles and at two time points. We identified previously uncharacterized skeletal muscle regions associated with myofiber type and tested the effect of human-specific and chimpanzee-specific mutations within these regions on gene expression. Identifying the parts of the human genome that code for our unique traits and studying how these regions of the genome vary across primates is key to understanding how these traits evolved. In addition, datasets and pipelines generated for this research will be of use to researchers interested in characterizing the regulatory landscape of other animal tissues and to researchers interested in muscle biology and disease.

Broader Impact

Humans are prone to a number of neuromuscular diseases that differentially affect fast (e.g., ALS) and slow (e.g., cachexia) myofibers. Datasets and findings from this project improve our understanding of muscle biology at the molecular level by identifying the genetic mechanisms controlling myofiber development. As such, this research may help target more efficient treatments (e.g., gene therapy) to reduce myofiber wasting, improving both quality of life and lifespan for millions of people.

The funded research has supported the training of a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Oregon. As part of this study, this graduate student has received advanced training in bioinformatics and genomics, and has gained considerable experience in these areas. This project has also provided her with the opportunity to set up, optimize, and run a cell culture lab, as well as train numerous undergraduates in aseptic cell culture technique. These skills and experiences have equipped her with a highly adaptable, and applicable, interdisciplinary toolkit that will enable her to pursue careers in STEM in both academia and industry. In addition, this project has given her the opportunity to present and publish her findings in both professional and public settings. She continues to incorporate aspects of her research when teaching and participating in science outreach events, which has increased student educational experiences and generated interest in STEM. This research has also enabled her to grow her professional network to include a group of highly successful colleagues with different skill sets, perspectives, and connections. This network has enhanced her professional development and will be an asset when developing her post-degree career plans. Importantly, successful completion of this dissertation research will produce a Ph.D. that contributes to a STEM field and increase diversity within areas of research where women are currently underrepresented.

The funded research has increased student involvement in STEM by supporting the training of diverse undergraduate students completing research projects and receiving training in the cell culture lab. These experiences have given these students the skill sets necessary to pursue careers or to continue their education in STEM related fields (e.g., biological anthropology, genetic counseling, bioinformatics, evolutionary biology, genetics).

abstractText:
The University of Oregon’s Oregon Institute of Marine Biology (OIMB), located in Charleston OR, will host a Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) Site during the summers of 2020-2022. The program will support the participation of ten undergraduates in research projects during a nine-week summer internship each summer, involving a total of thirty students. Objectives of this REU site are to teach undergraduates how to conduct research into biological processes and to ensure they are aware of career pathways for marine scientists. The program offers research opportunities to students from 2-year colleges using a tiered learning model with pairs of students – one from a 4-year (4YC) and one from a 2-year college (2YC) - working with mentors to conduct research. Student participants are recruited via a national search and are provided with a stipend, housing and travel funding.

Research topics focus on biological interactions of marine organisms and their environment, or on aspects of development and reproduction of marine invertebrates. Interns will conduct research projects on cellular dynamics, development, ecology and evolution of larval and juvenile marine organisms, impacts of climate change on foraging ecology of dungeness crabs, evaluating long term changes in eelgrass communities, and molecular biodiversity. Activities will include field trips to intertidal sites, the University of Oregon main campus in Eugene, and various coastal habitats. Professional development sessions will provide training in resume writing, interviewing, preparing posters, giving presentations, using R for graphs and statistics, use of professional social media, and the importance of networking and broader impacts of research. Following a workshop on outreach to broader audiences, interns will serve as scientific experts at OIMB's Charleston Marine Life Center, a public aquarium and museum. Interns will be encouraged to present their posters at undergraduate research symposia at their home institutions and at an appropriate annual professional meeting.

Projects Outcomes EMBOC REU OCE-1950520                 

The Oregon Institute of Marine Biology (OIMB) ran an REU-site program during seven summers from 2017 to 2024, Exploration of Marine Biology on the Oregon Coast (EMBOC).  The outcomes described here cover the second of two 3-year grants.  For this second grant our program was delayed a year due to the Covid pandemic (2020).  We offered our program for four summers, 2021-24 because we obtained a supplement that was combined with remaining funds to allow a cohort of six interns in 2024.

Each summer we engaged 6-11 interns (38 total) in nine weeks of mentored research.  Twenty-five interns from 4yr colleges and 13 interns from 2yr colleges worked in pairs in a tiered learning model in research laboratories at OIMB and the South Slough National Estuarine Research Reserve.  The pairing of interns permitted them to support one another while they worked full-time on separate research projects with one of 11 mentors (including 3 graduate students). Our program worked toward our and NSF’s shared goal of increasing mentored research opportunities for groups underrepresented in STEM, by recruiting diverse cohorts of interns. 28 of 38 EMBOC interns identified with one or more groups underrepresented in STEM (e.g. Hispanic, African American, Asian American, Pacific Islander, multiracial, 1st generation or veteran).  Three interns among the 38 were supported with residual funds from the previous REU-site grant (OCE-1659477).  

In addition to research, cohorts of interns also participated in weekly professional develop workshops covering topics on using library resources, reading scientific literature, ethics in research, diversity and inclusivity in science, preparing CV’s, finding jobs and applying to graduate school, and science communication (e.g. creating and presenting scientific talks posters, conveying science to a broader public audience).   They also presented their research to a public audience in 2-hour sessions at the Charleston Marine Life Center associated with OIMB. Lastly, each intern wrote a weekly blog post describing their research challenges and triumphs, experience in professional development and social excursions on the Oregon Coast, see https://uoregonoimb-reu.weebly.com/.

Each intern produced and presented a scientific poster on their research project at the end of each summer to an audience including OIMB faculty, students, interested members of the SW Oregon scientific community, and the public.  Twenty-three of 38 interns (including 9 from 2yr colleges) also attended and presented their research at regional or national scientific meetings.  Two of these interns won recognition at their scientific meetings for their research posters. 

Comparative surveys of interns conducted at the beginning and end of each summer showed that almost all interns gained significant understanding of how science is done: gains in their perceived research skills and confidence in ability to conduct meaningful research. Interns also 
reported change in educational and career goals toward pursuing graduate degrees and
careers in STEM fields and were very pleased to have been part of this learning and research experience.

At the time of this report (June 2025), 12 of 13 interns from 2YR colleges transferred to 4YR colleges and 1 is still in 2YR college.  30 interns of 38 in the four cohorts continued with some research, 10 went on to graduate school, 14 had STEM related jobs and two others had non-STEM jobs after our program. 

This was the last of two consecutive EMBOC REU-site grants that worked with 7 summer cohorts (2017-2024, but not 2020), totaling 71 interns (40 students from four-year institutions and 31 from two-year institutions).  In winter 2025, we sent surveys to all interns asking how their REU experience; we received 44 responses (62%).  When asked if the EMBOC program was helpful in developing the student’s science culture and skills, the percentages that answered   “strongly agreed” with these statements are shown:
1. Helped me gain skills in developing and testing a research question. 90%
2. Provided opportunities to improve my science communication skills. 88%
3. Provided professional development opportunities I used later in my education or career. 72%
4. Had a positive impact on my professional life. 84%
5. Had a positive impact on my educational and/or career track. 90%
6. Increased my professional network. 60%

We also asked how the EMBOC program influenced career decisions.  The percentages that reported agreeing or strongly agreeing (respectively) with the statements are shown:
1.    Influenced my decision to pursue a career that involves research. 26% 58%
2.    Influenced my decision to pursue a career in STEM. 23% 70%
3.    Influenced my decision to pursue a teaching career. 26% 16%
4.    Influenced my decision to pursue a non-STEM career. 2% 2%
5.    Did not influence my decision to pursue my career path. 0% 2%.

abstractText:
Pyroclastic density currents (PDCs) are hot mixtures of eruption-derived particles and gas that move laterally along the ground.  PDCs are commonly generated by eruption column or lava dome collapse and are driven by negative buoyancy.   Due to their mobility, rapid velocities, and high temperatures, PDCs are the most hazardous volcanic phenomena and are responsible for over 50% of volcanic-related fatalities. PDCs are also challenging to observe directly.  In addition to their hazardous nature, PDCs occur infrequently and often are located in remote and inhospitable places.  Furthermore, direct visual observations can usually only be made  of  the  outer  shell  of  the  flow  as  the complex internal dynamics are obscured by visually opaque fluid.  Therefore, most of our understanding about these multiphase, turbulent flows comes from geological observations of PDC deposits, laboratory studies and numerical models. This work extends knowledge of PDC dynamics by associating physical processes with seismic and infrasonic waves. Geophysical observations (infrasound and seismic) can be made at safe distances from PDC activity and can provide high-resolution information about PDC dynamics. This project also supports a postdoctoral scholar, who will engage in activities that bring STEM and natural hazard resources to schools in the Cascadia region.

For this project we will be developing a quantitative framework to relate PDC properties and dynamics to geophysical observables. The researchers will perform 3D multiphase simulations of PDCs and compute the infrasound and seismic radiation. This will enable the investigators to directly compare the simulation outputs with field data, which will provide a way to validate and improve numerical models of PDC dynamics.  The researchers will perform a sensitivity analysis to understand what properties the geophysical observables are sensitive to and will explore the geophysical signals of different physical processes that have been shown to be important to PDC dynamics, such entrainment and fluidization.  The proposed work will increase fundamental scientific understanding about the processes governing PDCs and will aid in data interpretation and volcano monitoring efforts by developing quantitative links between geophysical observables and flow properties.

projectOutComesReport:
Pyroclastic density currents (PDCs) are the most hazardous volcanic phenomena and are responsible for over 50% of volcano-related fatalities. PDCs are hot mixtures of eruption-derived particles and gas that are generated by collapse of an eruption column or lava dome and can travel large distances at great velocities. Our understanding of the processes governing these complex, multiphase and turbulent flows is limited because PDCs are dangerous and challenging to observe directly. However, PDC activity frequently generates geophysical signals - infrasound (low frequency acoustic waves) in the atmosphere and seismic waves in the solid Earth - that can be safely recorded at remote distances. In recent years, there have been an increasing number of geophysical observations of PDC activity. Much of this work has been observational and there remains no quantitative framework to relate PDC properties to the observed geophysical signals.

 

This grant supported postdoctoral researcher who modified a numerical model to simulate PDC dynamics and computed the associated infrasound and seismic radiation. This grant led to the development of integral methods to examine infrasound from both plume and PDC sources. Further, multiphase flow models of PDC were coupled to this approach to link propagated acoustic signals with flow conditions. Further work was done using discrete element simulations that can resolve individual particles to compute numerous individual collisions with the ground to better examine seismic sources. These detailed source-physics models have been coupled to both wave form simulations and to empirical approaches to examine the seismic radiation from these sources.

 

This work aids the interpretation of data from hazardous volcanoes, and provides valuable information for planning future instrument deployments. The simulation framework developed here can also now be applicable to other particle-laden gravity currents, such as lahars, debris flows and turbidity currents. Validation of numerical approaches for PDC dynamics remains a topic of intense interest. Previous studies have compared simulation results to geological observations of PDC deposits but these only provide an incomplete snapshot of the complex and time-varying processes governing PDC dynamics. Validation work has also been done recently on large scale experiments, some large enough to produce measurable geophysical signals. The work done here enables PDC simulations to be directly compared to geophysical observables, which will improve model validation. In addition to the broader impact of developing better tools to interpret the signals from hazardous flows, this work resulted in material that was used for outreach to elementary school classrooms, and in the training of a postdoctoral researcher.

abstractText:
The coronavirus pandemic provides a rare opportunity to study public risk perceptions and risk-related behaviors in the midst of a World Health Organization Public Health Emergency of International Concern that could threaten the quality of life of a wide spectrum of Americans. Few emergencies within the United States have affected so many people. The situation is a rich opportunity because it is occurring in real-time and is highly dynamic, involving many players in our country and around the world. As a result, it allows the research team a chance to compare this health threat with other perceived disasters such as immigration, terrorism, and possible future public health emergencies. The public’s perceptions and risk-related behaviors seem likely to change over time in response to media coverage as well as actions from our own and foreign governments.

In one longitudinal study, the research team invites participants from Amazon Mechanical Turk to complete one survey each month for 5 months. The researchers query their risk perceptions and affective responses toward the coronavirus, frequency of discussions about the coronavirus with others, behavioral intentions towards hypothetical experimental vaccines and treatments, and support for possible policy solutions such as quarantine. The research also ascertains their intended travel plans and media exposure to the pandemic including how much they trust those sources. The team models the emotional, risk-perception, and behavioral responses of participants toward the coronavirus by using a latent variable growth curve model that examines the trajectories of variables over time. To establish causal links, the scholars also conduct a second related experiment that manipulates affect through narratives and examines its effects on risk perceptions, medical decisions, and policy decisions. Participants are assigned to a more negative or less negative condition, and mediation analysis is used to evaluate the manipulation’s effects. In these studies, theoretical links are made between risk perceptions, social amplification of risk, the affect heuristic and other functions of affect, and numeracy. There is a dynamic test of the three functions of affect by correlating current feelings over time with risk judgments, intended prevention and treatment behaviors, and support for policy options. Theoretical research on affect has not been tested in the setting of a world health emergency. This research results in deep mechanistic understanding of how emotions and media exposure influence vaccine and treatment choices as well as support for policies. Finally, the second study establishes causal links between affect and support for prevention, treatment, and policy strategies. The research tests the dynamic and causal power of the functions of affect and motivated reasoning in order to lay the groundwork for interventions for emotional responses to the coronavirus and future epidemics. The research also has important implications, including for communication methods, for other affect-rich decisions faced by the public and policy makers.

projectOutComesReport:
One of the historical and central challenges of risk perception research has been the difficulty of examining how people?s attitudes and behavior in real-time emergencies change over time. We proposed to study how people perceive and react to the COVID-19 crisis, what information they attend to, who they trust (or do not trust), and how this crisis affects future plans, choices of preventive and treatment options, and support for policy options.

 We tracked a panel of 1,284 respondents from late February 2020 to December 2020. Across six waves of data collection, we measured affective (emotional) responses to the epidemic, perceptions of risk, and risk-related decisions and behaviors, including support for policies. We also conducted an experiment (described later) to test whether affect towards disease had causal effects on low-value treatment choices.

Six main findings emerged.

  1. Trust in doctors and scientists. Doctors and clinicians, scientists, and the CDC were consistently trusted by most of our sample from March to December. In contrast, President Trump, the news media, and the American public were distrusted by the majority of our sample (Figure 1). Thus, most people still trust doctors and scientists, who are critical sources of public health information. 
  2. Political polarization. We documented worrying impacts of political ideology on risk perceptions and negative affect (Figure 2). Conservatives also were more likely than liberals to endorse anti-Chinese conspiracies and to dehumanize Asians and Asian Americans, while being less likely to take protective behaviors.
  3. Motivated verbal ability rather than motivated numeracy. Political polarization was shown more by people with higher than lower verbal ability (controlling for numeric ability) as indicated by their affect and perceived risk concerning COVID-19 and policy attitudes. This result was surprising because prior work, including in our lab, implicated numeric ability as potentially the cause of greater polarization. These latest findings may explain why some researchers have not replicated previous motivated numeracy findings?it was verbal ability rather than numeric ability that was more likely to predict increased polarization. However, those higher in verbal ability were better, however, than those lower at rejecting misinformation. People higher in ability may have become more polarized because of their consumption of partisan news media (e.g., conservative Fox News vs. liberal New York Times) and interpretation of COVID-relevant information (Figure 3). Thus, providing more information will not necessarily reduce polarization, because higher-ability people may interpret it to preserve their current beliefs.
  4. Affect may drive COVID-19 reactions. We also documented longitudinal evidence for multiple functions of affect?negative affect in self-report and text analysis of participant writing samples about coronavirus?being associated with greater perceived risk (affect as information), more attention toward news about the pandemic (affect as a spotlight), and more support for protective behaviors and policies (affect as a motivator of behavior).
  5. Affect-motivated choosing. We also conducted an experiment to test whether affect might cause these effects. However, instead of conducting the experiment with COVID-19?due to concerns about whether we could alter affect towards COVID-19 and if it was ethical given that we expected it to change subsequent behavior?we tested our hypotheses in the context of an uncommon disease-causing microbe, Naegleria fowleri,(colloquially referred to as the brain-eating amoeba). We randomly assigned participants to receive information that would increase or decrease their negative affect towards the microbe. Participants in the greater-negative-affect condition subsequently reported more positive affect towards a drug that could treat the disease than those in the lower-negative-affect condition. Critically, they were more interested in and optimistic about using the drug to prevent the disease (which it is not designed to do). Our findings imply that fear of COVID-19 may have contributed to interest in low-value treatments and preventatives (e.g., ivermectin).
  6. Providing numeric likelihoods and offering choice encourages vaccine interest. In a series of studies, we demonstrated that providing information about multiple brands of vaccines reduced intentions to vaccinate if participants were not allowed to choose their preferred vaccine. We further questioned in a separate study the costs of standard practice?not providing numeric likelihood information about vaccine side effects. Providing those numbers (e.g., ?7% experienced fever?) increased comprehension and vaccination intentions. Furthermore, giving people both numeric likelihoods and interpretative labels (e.g., ?common?) particularly increased vaccine intentions among vaccine-hesitant people (Figure 4).

Altogether, our research has contributed to the scientific understanding of how people responded to the ongoing COVID-19 crisis and how public health officials can communicate to better encourage self-protective behaviors, such as vaccines.

abstractText:
The gut microbiome is the community of bacteria that resides in the gastrointestinal tract, and past research has demonstrated that this community is physiologically important to its host. However, researchers do not yet fully understand why the gut microbiome varies so much from individual to individual. This doctoral dissertation project will examine how social behaviors such as physical proximity and infant care-giving affect gut microbiome transmission among adult and infant individuals in a wild primate population. This research will therefore advance fundamental knowledge about microbiome variation in a non-human primate and may also inform microbiome research in humans. The project will facilitate the completion of a doctoral degree by a woman in science, contribute to the training of multiple undergraduate students in scientific laboratory and field methods, and engage young women and other underrepresented groups in STEM through public outreach. In addition, the work will provide wildlife education to local school children, ecotourists, tour guides, and field assistants near the research site through training and public outreach, which will increase local human resource capacity and aid in the conservation of a critically endangered primate species. 

A mounting body of evidence suggests that the gut microbiome is an important phenotypic trait in understanding human biological variation and well-being. However, we still lack a necessary understanding of the factors that shape phenotypic and developmental plasticity in this trait. A primary factor affecting variation in the gut microbiome that remains unclear is the longitudinal effect of social environment on the composition of the gut microbiome. Further, we do not understand how socially-mediated transmission affects the assembly of the gut microbiome during development, which is a critical window thought to have long-reaching effects later in life. The primate model system allows examination of how the gut microbiome changes with shifting social dynamics because adult female social bonds are known to fluctuate following infant births and infants receive variable amounts of social contact via allomaternal care (caretaking behaviors by individuals other than the mother). Using a combination of detailed behavioral data and microbial DNA sequencing in longitudinally collected fecal samples, this research will determine the effect size of social transmission of gut microbes among socially interacting adult females and between allomothers and infants.

projectOutComesReport:
Project Outcome Report

The gut microbiome is the community of microscopic organisms that reside in an individual’s gastrointestinal tract. Although this community has been implicated in a variety of human health outcomes and is known to be critical to proper immune system development, we still don’t have a complete understanding of what shapes gut microbiome variation among individuals. While prior research has demonstrated that social environment has an impact, when this begins and how it changes through time remains a gap in knowledge. This is an important topic to address as humans undergo a variety of social experiences starting at a young age that could impact gut microbiome variation and ultimately health outcomes. Our goals were thus to determine 1) how differences in social environment affect gut microbiome variation through infant development, and 2) how change in social environment affects the adult gut microbiome over time. We accomplished this through detailed simultaneous characterization of gut microbiome variation and social interactions in infant, juvenile, and adult individuals in a wild colobus monkey population (Colobus vellerosus) in Ghana (Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary) over a 2 year time period. These monkeys are an ideal model for addressing this topic as they are closely related to humans, display complex patterns of sociality, allow for comprehensive behavioral and biological sample collection, and they are known to display high levels of allocare – or infant care performed by adults other than the mother. There is also variation in this infant care so that some infants receive more than others, and adult female social bonds are dynamic and can change rapidly in the presence of an infant.

We found colobus developmental gut microbiome patterns are similar to those seen in humans and many other primates. However, we found the infant and juvenile individuals had gut microbiomes more like those of the adults in their own group compared to the adults of other groups. Furthermore, infants with a mother positioned more centrally in a group’s social network had more adult-like gut microbiomes, as did infants that received allocare from more individuals. These results provide further evidence of the impact of social interactions during infanthood, which is of particular interest as infancy represents a crucial time period during which gut microbial variation can have significant consequences for long-term health. For the adult colobus females, we found that increased social interactions (specifically higher grooming rates) followed infant birth, and these were reflected in greater gut microbial similarity among adult female social group members during this time. This demonstrates that that even relatively short-lived changes in social relationships may cause shifts in the microbiome.

Taken together, these results expand our understanding of how social factors shape the gut microbiome across the lifespan, particularly in animals that interact socially and live in multi-generational groups. This includes humans, which can display large caregiving networks during infant development with constantly changing social networks throughout life. Infants of such animals have rich social lives that include non-parental adults that can impact their microbiomes. Further, the effects of these infant-adult social relationships are not unidirectional; infants also impact the social lives of adults, which in turn affects the adult microbiomes as well. These results provide a more comprehensive understanding of how social influences might mediate human microbial variation and could have important implications for the social determinants of human health. This work also demonstrates the utility of natural non-human primate research, as habituated populations studied longitudinally offer particularly advantageous model systems in which natural experiments can help scientists disentangle complex social and biological dynamics.

More broadly, this research contributes to a growing body of work focused on the biology and behavior of Colobus vellerosus, a critically endangered primate at risk of extinction. The study population is the only known stable population of C. vellerosus left in the world (approximately 400 individuals), and this research provides preliminary information that future research can build upon to examine the health and wellbeing of these dwindling monkeys. In addition, the field component of this research helped support the livelihoods of Ghanian field assistants and involved outreach to local communities, both of which aid in preventing the extintion of this species and loss of this forest. Lastly, this research led to the direct training of three American women who are continuing in the workforce as scientists - two of whom conducted undergraduate honors theses and earned their Bachelor of Science Degrees and one of whom conducted a doctoral dissertation and earned her PhD. As part of the supplemental funding included in this project, the doctoral student obtained internship experience at a non-academic institution, which facilitated her ability to secure employment in the non-profit zoological job sector as a conservation scientist.

abstractText:
In order for speech communication to be successful speakers must be able to deliver their messages clearly to their listeners. For example, when a listener does not understand what was said by a speaker the first time, the speaker may repeat what they said in a clearer manner so that the listener can understand it. This seemingly simple act of enhancing intelligibility of speech for a listener is often carried out naturally by fluent speakers of the language, yet it can be difficult for people who produce less fluent and less intelligible speech, such as non-native speakers of the language. Not being understood by listeners has very real consequences for non-native speakers as it can significantly decrease their opportunities to obtain jobs and education, and more broadly, to participate in society as an equal member. The significance of this issue is highlighted by the growing population of non-native English speakers in the U.S. This project seeks to better understand why it can be difficult to enhance speech intelligibility in a non-native language by examining how speakers of different linguistic backgrounds use speech enhancement strategies in different communication contexts. The results of this project could inform the development of methodologies for second language learning as well as interventions for clinical populations who may experience difficulty enhancing their speech intelligibility. 

The goal of this project is to understand two aspects of what contributes to enhancing speech intelligibility: what kinds of strategies speakers use to enhance their speech and how these strategies are perceived by listeners. Specifically, the proposed experiments examine how a speaker’s ability to speak clearly is affected by different sources, such as the speaker's language background, characteristics of the speech materials (e.g., familiarity of the words or phrases), and characteristics of the communication context. Further, the project examines how speakers' attempts to enhance speech intelligibility translate to listeners' perception of this speech, including perceived degree of comprehensibility (how easy it is to understand the speech) and perceived degree of speaker effort (how hard the speaker is trying to speak clearly). This project will help us better understand the contributions from both speakers and listeners to enhancing speech intelligibility for a variety of native and non-native speaking populations.

projectOutComesReport:
One important factor that contributes to successful speech communication is an individual’s ability to speak more clearly when their listeners do not understand their speech. Though native talkers are able to implement various acoustic-phonetic speech enhancements to make their speech more understandable to their listeners (e.g., by speaking more slowly, loudly, or by articulating sounds more clearly in speech enhancements), such goal-oriented adaptations employed by non-native talkers are much less well-understood. This project investigated how talkers’ ability to implement speech enhancements is shaped by their target language experience and how these enhancements impact listeners’ perception.

The current work provided novel contributions that inform production and perception of speech enhancements. In terms of production, we demonstrated that talkers’ ability to implement goal-oriented acoustic-phonetic modifications was generally impacted by their target language experience; native talkers and higher-proficiency non-native talkers were better able to modify characteristics of their speech and enhance intelligibility for listeners as compared to lower-proficiency non-native talkers. This suggests that lower-proficiency talkers have not acquired the range of stylistic variations as much as higher-proficiency talkers and native talkers have.

The current work also revealed that perceptual benefits resulting from speech enhancements differed depending on how listeners were asked to evaluate the speech, such that native talkers’ and higher-proficiency talkers’ clear speech enhancements that resulted in an intelligibility improvement did not improve perceived comprehensibility (i.e., how easy to understand the speech). However, those clear speech enhancements robustly improved listeners’ perceived degree of talker effort (i.e., how hard the talker is trying to speak clearly); the robust improvement in perceived degree of talker effort was also observed in perception of lower-proficiency talkers’ clear speech enhancements.

By examining both acoustic properties and perceptual consequences of speech enhancements, the current work has provided a unique contribution to the growing body of work on speech adaptation. Specifically, the findings suggest that native and non-native talkers have the flexibility to accommodate listeners’ communicative needs, and that this flexibility is shaped by the combination of talkers’ linguistic backgrounds and the focus of adaptation. Furthermore, multi-faceted nature of speech perception needs to be accounted for when evaluating perceptual benefits of speech enhancements. Thus, as a whole, this project has provided insights into, and has raised new questions about, the mechanisms for goal-oriented phonetic adaptations as well as perceptual consequences of these adaptations. The current results have implications for how second language proficiency may be defined, such that knowing how to manipulate acoustic-phonetic properties of the speech to increase intelligibility, in addition to being able to produce intelligible speech in general, is part of what characterizes talkers’ language proficiency. Going forward, considering both talker-related and listener-related factors in speech enhancements is not only relevant but also critical to building successful communication in the increasingly multi-lingual and multi-cultural society.

abstractText:
Volcanic eruptions have to potential to threaten agriculture, infrastructure, aviation, and human life at local to global scales. These events represent the intersection of geologic processes that proceed over thousands to millions of years and destabilization of the volcanic reservoir which may occur rapidly over only days to years. These processes may be interrogated through retrospective geologic studies of past eruptions and geophysical monitoring, respectively. This project is focused on integrating these approaches at the Three Sisters Volcanic Complex, a “very high threat potential” volcanic system located in the western United States. The goals are to elucidate hazards specific to the Three Sisters through the investigation of recent eruptions and volcanic unrest and produce new conceptual and quantitative models that can be applied to understand the hazards and improve eruption forecasting for active volcanoes globally. The results of this project will be disseminated to the general public through animation and videos published on-line and a self-guided geology hiking guide made available to the many recreational visitors to the Three Sister’s Wilderness Area.

Linking the processes that catalyze the growth, evolution, destabilization, and eruption of magma reservoirs to their expression as observable unrest represents an important scientific frontier that requires inter-disciplinary collaborations across the geosciences. Parallel advances in geophysics, petrochronology, and numerical modeling have made substantial contributions to the understanding of magma reservoir processes. Yet, these methods remain poorly integrated. The unusual confluence of frequent late Pleistocene to late Holocene eruptions, which range in composition from basaltic andesite to rhyolite, with modern volcanic unrest make the Three Sisters a prime natural laboratory at which to pursue this integrated approach. This project will produce new crystal-scale petrochronologic data for lavas and associated explosive products erupted from the Three Sisters Volcanic Complex, central Oregon Cascades, during the last ca. 50,000 yr. These data will inform interpretations of: 1) the petrogenesis of the rhyolite and dacite lavas erupted at the Three Sisters and if there is a genetic relationship between these rock types; 2) the longevity and physical integration of the magma reservoir(s) that produced the late Pleistocene flare-up of intermediate and silicic volcanism; and 3) the nature and tempo of the processes that preceded, and potentially triggered, these eruptions. In parallel, a high-resolution Bouguer gravity survey will be conducted to constrain the physical structure of the modern magma reservoir. These new geochemical and geophysical data will be integrated with the existing geodetic observations of recent uplift in coupled models of magma dynamics and crustal deformation. Accordingly, these observations and models will quantitatively test if recent unrest at Three Sisters reflects similar processes to those associated with the late-Pleistocene volcanism.

abstractText:
The Cascadia subduction zone is known to generate infrequent (every ~500 years) but potentially very large (up to magnitude 9) earthquakes. The most recent such earthquake occurred on January 26th, 1700, and GPS data acquired during the last two decades suggest that strain is accumulating across the subduction zone fault in preparation for a future earthquake. However, there is considerable uncertainty about how the geologic structure of the subduction zone will impact strain release during a Cascadia earthquake. Different plausible earthquake scenarios result in quite different predicted ground shaking, which in turn influences building codes and emergency response plans. This project will image the structure of the crust in the region where large Cascadia earthquakes are thought to occur. The objective is to understand three-dimensional variations in seismic velocity in order to provide insights into the factors that control segmentation of slip during earthquakes and the resulting amplitude of ground shaking in populated areas and sedimentary basins. With its large footprint and involvement of many field hands, this project will provide student research experiences and opportunities for public outreach and education about geohazards in the Pacific Northwest. This project is a collaboration between Oregon State University, University of Oregon, Eugene, South Dakota School of Mines and Technology and the U.S. Geological Survey.

This project has the ultimate goal of generating a high-resolution model of an active subduction system that will span the Cascadia plate boundary, including the transition between major along-strike segments, and cross the transition from the nominally locked zone down-dip to depths where plate motion is accommodated by episodic tremor and slip. A dense network of temporary short-period seismometers along the coast of the Pacific Northwest will extend high resolution imaging of the structure of the overlying and down-going plates, as well as the thickness and characteristics of material within the plate interface zone, to depths that are critical for understanding earthquake processes. The array design includes a single deployment of three-component instruments at 1-km intervals along the onshore extension of dip lines embedded within a sparser grid of seismometers spaced 7-10 km apart for a total of ~700 three-component seismic stations. To tie results from the seismogenic part of the plate boundary to larger-scale forearc and arc structure, two profiles will extend across the forearc. All stations will record natural sources as well as man-made sources for the duration of the deployment. The seismic data from this experiment will be made immediately available to the community. The resulting high-resolution 3D Vp model will also be made accessible and is critical for constraining analyses of seismic noise, magnetotelluric and potential field data, as well as for improving predictions of earthquake ground shaking and tsunami generation in the Pacific Northwest.
